title: Secure Handling of Untrusted Contributions
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of secure handling of untrusted contributions and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to secure handling of untrusted contributions.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on secure handling of untrusted contributions. Forked pull requests and other untrusted contributions must not execute attacker-controlled code in jobs that hold secrets or powerful write permissions. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Secure Handling of Untrusted Contributions matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Forked pull requests and other untrusted contributions must not execute attacker-controlled code in jobs that hold secrets or powerful write permissions. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Forked pull requests and other untrusted contributions must not execute attacker-controlled code in jobs that hold secrets or powerful write permissions. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Forked pull requests
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Restricted secrets for untrusted workflows
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: pull_request and pull_request_target differences
items.text: For pull_request and pull_request_target differences, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Untrusted branch and commit data
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Privileged workflow risks
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Avoiding execution of untrusted code with powerful credentials
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

content_blocks.code:
name: Validate untrusted pull requests without secrets
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run non-privileged checks
        run: echo "Replace with the project test command; do not expose deploy secrets"
content_blocks.expected_output: A pull request targeting `main` runs read-only validation without deployment credentials. In a real workflow, review checkout ref behavior and dependencies before executing contributor-controlled code.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the secret/variable scope and permissions match your environment before a real run.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove the temporary workflow and revoke test credentials or app installations when finished.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to secure handling of untrusted contributions. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain secure handling of untrusted contributions, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Constrain credentials and token permissions, and prefer scoped, short-lived authentication where supported.

content.task: Apply secure handling of untrusted contributions to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Forked pull requests and other untrusted contributions must not execute attacker-controlled code in jobs that hold secrets or powerful write permissions.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: A pull request targeting `main` runs read-only validation without deployment credentials. In a real workflow, review checkout ref behavior and dependencies before executing contributor-controlled code.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.

Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available.
